name: Hypochlorous acid spray

lead: A hypochlorous acid (HOCl) spray is a mild antimicrobial mist used on skin. HOCl is the same chemical neutrophils make to kill microbes. Acne-prone users spray it to reduce bacteria and soothe irritation for calmer, clearer-looking skin.

HOCl oxidises microbial proteins and damages membranes. In one study, an HOCl eyelid solution cut staphylococci by over 99% in 20 minutes. Since 2016 the US FDA has cleared products with HOCl as the main active for wounds and infections. No studies of cosmetic outcomes such as acne were identified.

paras: People mist it onto cleansed skin, or onto the chest and back, once or twice a day, often after workouts or shaving and before moisturizer. It is used as a gentle add-on to an existing routine and is also common after procedures such as microneedling.
The EPA classes it as non-hazardous, though as an oxidiser it can irritate depending on concentration. Solutions degrade and lose potency with time, heat and light, so shelf life is short.

angle.text: Acne-prone users mist hypochlorous acid on face or body to reduce bacteria and soothe irritation, for calmer, clearer-looking skin. It has regulatory clearance and studies in wound and eyelid care.

lead: Hypochlorous acid (HOCl) spray is a mist containing a dilute solution of hypochlorous acid, a weak acid that forms when chlorine dissolves in water. It is marketed as a skin-safe antimicrobial for face and body care [1].

HOCl is also made naturally by neutrophils, which use it to kill microbes [1]. Since 2016 the US FDA has cleared products with HOCl as the main active ingredient for treating wounds and infections, and it is approved as a saline preservative [1]. No clinical studies of HOCl sprays for cosmetic appearance outcomes such as acne were identified.
infobox: Short; solutions degrade to salt water [1]

paras: HOCl oxidises sulfur-containing proteins in microbes, causing cross-linking and aggregation, and damages membranes and energy production [1].

Uses described include wound care, eyelid hygiene, and disinfection sprays and wipes [1]. A 2017 study reported that a saline eyelid solution preserved with HOCl cut staphylococci by over 99% after 20 minutes without disrupting overall bacterial diversity, and it was non-irritating on testing [1]. A 2025 case report of refractory dry eye disease lists hypochlorous acid spray among earlier treatments that gave limited relief [2].

The US EPA classifies it as non-hazardous, though as an oxidiser it may irritate or corrode depending on concentration and pH [1]. Solutions lose potency over time, and storage away from heat and light slows this [1].
No studies found for appearance or acne outcomes of HOCl sprays. Studies noted above concern eyelid hygiene and wound care [1][2].

timeline.event: FDA begins approving HOCl-based wound and infection treatments [1].
